title: Some Perspective — the guided walkthrough

slides.title: India grew. Did that growth buy what it was supposed to?
slides.body: Between 2014 and 2026 India became the world's most populous country and its fourth-largest economy. Over the same years, every available measure of democratic quality fell. This walkthrough sets out what the data shows about whether those two facts were a trade — and concludes that they were not.
slides.note: Use the arrow keys, or swipe. Every figure here is read live from the site's dataset.

slides.title: The bargain: constraint traded for prosperity
slides.body: The strongest case for the period runs like this. A decisive executive, unencumbered by coalition bargaining, judicial review and federal veto points, can do things a constrained one cannot. Institutional constraint is the price; material progress is what it buys.
points: That is a serious argument, and this project tests it rather than dismissing it.
A bargain requires both halves to be measured: what was given up, and what was received.
Most accounts measure only one half.

slides.title: The instruments needed to check also degraded
slides.body: Assessing performance after 2014 runs into a specific difficulty: the statistical apparatus that would register the answer was itself weakened during the period.
points: The 2021 census was postponed and still has not been conducted.
The 2017-18 consumption survey was completed, then withheld after it showed rural consumption falling.
The national accounts were rebased in 2015 in a way that lowered earlier growth and raised later growth — never independently reviewed.
Two statistical commissioners resigned; the NSSO was merged into the NSO.
Official COVID mortality was ~0.5 million against independent excess-mortality estimates of 3-5 million.
slides.note: Each is individually documented. What makes the pattern notable is that the withheld numbers were, with high consistency, the unfavourable ones.

slides.title: Three indices, one script, both eras
slides.body: To compare the UPA decade (2004-2013) with the NDA period (2014-2026) fairly, both are measured by the same instrument — a single deterministic script applied across the whole period. Any difference is a difference in inputs, not in method.
points: SSI — Statistical Suppression Index, 0-10. Interference with official statistics.
FCI — Fiscal Centralisation Index, 0-1. Fiscal authority shifting from states to the union.
DQI — Democratic Quality Index, 0-1. Four published third-party democracy measures combined.

slides.title: Every index moves the same way after 2014
slides.body: SSI is zero across the entire UPA decade, peaks at {{max:economic.ssi}} in 2021-22, and is still {{last:economic.ssi}} in 2026. FCI rises from {{first:eraHistory.fci}} to {{last:economic.fci}}. DQI falls from {{first:eraHistory.dqi}} to {{last:economic.dqi}}.
slides.note: The shaded band marks the NDA period. SSI is shown on its own 0-10 scale.

slides.title: From zero to nine, and it has not returned to zero
slides.body: The SSI weights six documented streams by how much each damages the public's ability to evaluate the government: the census delay carries the most weight, then the mortality undercount, then the withheld consumption survey, the disputed GDP revision, the loss of institutional independence, and the employment-data delay.
points: No qualifying event occurred in 2004-2013, so that decade scores zero.
The 2021-22 peak of {{max:economic.ssi}} is these streams stacking, not one event.
It settles at {{last:economic.ssi}} because the damage is structural: the census is still outstanding and the NSO merger was never reversed.

slides.kicker: The first half of the bargain
slides.title: Growth did not accelerate
slides.body: Real GDP growth averaged {{avg:eraHistory.gdpGrowth}}% across 2004-2013 and {{avg:economic.gdpGrowth}}% across 2014-2026.
points: The later figure includes the 2020 pandemic contraction, which accounts for much of the gap.
But the two periods are not cleanly comparable at all: the 2015 rebasing moved measured growth in the government's favour, and was never independently reviewed.
Even taking the official numbers at face value, no acceleration is visible.

slides.title: Twelve straight years of falling formal employment
slides.body: The share of workers with any social-security cover fell from {{first:economic.formalEmployment}}% in 2014 to {{last:economic.formalEmployment}}% in 2026 — down or flat in every single year, while GDP grew throughout.
slides.note: This is the most consistent multi-year pattern in the dataset, and it does not depend on the disputed national accounts.

slides.title: The growth happened where the jobs are not
slides.body: Agriculture holds 42% of employment while producing 18% of output. Manufacturing — the sector that in the standard development sequence absorbs that labour — holds only 11% of jobs.
slides.note: Industrial policy weighted toward capital-intensive sectors raises output more than payroll. Electronics generates roughly one job per ₹1.5 crore invested; garments, at comparable investment, generate vastly more.

slides.title: The bottom half lost about an eighth of its share
slides.body: The top 1% share rose from {{first:economic.top1Share}}% to {{last:economic.top1Share}}%. The bottom 50% share fell from {{first:economic.bottom50Share}}% to {{last:economic.bottom50Share}}%.
slides.note: The top-end level matters more than its movement: at {{last:economic.top1Share}}%, it is the highest recorded since 1922. The sharper decade change is at the bottom.

slides.title: The one exception, and why it isn't a win
slides.body: Consumer price inflation averaged {{avg:eraHistory.cpiInflation}}% in 2004-2013 against {{avg:economic.cpiInflation}}% in 2014-2026. It is the only measure moving the other way — and it is mostly not about Indian policy at all.
points: The comparison straddles a global commodity cycle. Brent crude fell from about $115 a barrel in mid-2014 to under $30 by early 2016, driven by US shale supply and OPEC defending market share. India imports about 86% of its crude.
An external shock that size, landing exactly at the boundary between the two periods, explains more of the gap than any change of government does.
Where domestic policy did help, it was inflation targeting — a rule that binds the executive's hands. That is delegation, not concentration.
And the 2026 figure sits on a new CPI basket where food's weight fell from 45.9% to 36.8%, so it prints lower for the same price movements.
slides.note: The full argument — six factors, the strongest case against us, and what would change our reading — is at someperspective.info/inflation.

slides.title: Eight of nine measures worse; one better
slides.body: Comparing period averages across every directly comparable measure, the later period performs worse on eight and better on one.
slides.note: If the later period's statistics are biased in the government's favour — as the SSI argues — then this comparison understates the deterioration rather than overstating it.

slides.title: A decline comparable to Turkey's, from a higher base
slides.body: India's V-Dem Liberal Democracy Index fell from 0.488 to 0.260 over the period, a fall of 0.228 points. Turkey fell from 0.252 to 0.110; Hungary from 0.521 to 0.315. Turkey's proportional fall is steeper, from a base already near the floor; India's is the largest absolute fall of the three.
slides.note: Brazil and South Africa, large democracies under real political stress over the same years, moved comparatively little. Whatever is happening in the measure globally, it is not marking everyone down.

slides.title: A different method reaches the same conclusion
slides.body: Kevin and Robin Grier (Texas Tech) build a synthetic counterfactual — a weighted blend of comparator countries fitted to India's path over 1984-2013 — and measure the gap that opens after 2014. All ten governance indicators they test deteriorate, every one at a joint p-value of 0.00.
slides.note: Different method, different data, different authors, no shared machinery with this project. Their electoral-democracy gap of -60.2% sits close to the -63.4% raw decline measured here — though the two are not the same quantity.

slides.title: The limits, stated plainly
slides.body: This project is descriptive. It establishes what happened on both dimensions; it does not identify a causal effect of governance on growth.
points: The author is a Manmohan Singh Fellow of the All India Professionals' Congress, a department of the Indian National Congress, and this comparison runs in that party's favour. The interest is declared in full on the site; what is offered against it is that every input, every weighting and every step is published and can be recomputed.
The SSI's zero for the UPA decade is the most contestable number here — though the conclusion survives even a generous re-coding of that era.
The DQI inherits whatever biases exist in V-Dem, Freedom House and RSF.
The FCI is relative to its own sample and means nothing outside it.
The three indices are not independent evidence of one another — they plausibly measure one underlying process.
The window contains a pandemic, which supplies a legitimate reason for some of what the indices register.
slides.note: An error in this project's own documents — one that ran in its favour — was found and corrected in August 2026. It is reported in the paper rather than quietly fixed.

slides.title: Statistical independence is the first reform, not the fifth
slides.body: Every other question — whether growth accelerated, whether poverty fell, whether welfare reached anyone — can only be settled against evidence produced by institutions willing to publish unfavourable findings.
points: Conduct the census. Publish consumption surveys on a fixed cycle regardless of what they show.
Restore the separation between the statistical office and the ministry it evaluates.
Refer the disputed GDP back-series to independent review.
Then: formalisation of employment, an industrial policy weighted toward labour absorption, and an explicit settlement on fiscal federalism.
slides.note: A government that did everything else on this list while leaving the statistical system alone would leave the public unable to tell whether any of it worked.

slides.title: All of this is open, and checkable
slides.body: Every figure in this walkthrough is read live from the same dataset the site and the paper use. Nothing here is a screenshot.
